💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics.
  • Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.
  • Now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics. The computational models simulate excitation-inhibition balance across 90 connected brain regions, revealing distinct mechanistic signatures for Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal degeneration, and environmental exposures ranging from air pollution to democratic governance.

Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.

Now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr. Agustín Ibáñez (Scientific Director of BrainLat at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, strategic director of core scientific assets at the BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, and faculty at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin) and first author Dr. Rubén Herzog (BrainLat and Distinguished Professor at the University of the Balearic Islands) has transformed static brain scans into dynamic, personalized virtual laboratories.

Published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering, the study introduces biophysical “digital brain twins” constructed from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans of 6,986 individuals spanning ages 18 to 100 across 16 countries.

Rather than treating brain scans as passive statistical snapshots, biophysical brain twins apply mathematical equations grounded in neurobiology to simulate how populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact across 90 connected brain regions.

For each participant, the investigators tuned their computational model until its simulated fMRI output closely matched the individual’s actual resting-state brain recordings. Independent validation highlighted that model-derived regional excitability closely correlated with structural grey matter volume, confirming that the virtual simulations capture real biological architecture.

In a recent development, “Every brain ages in a different context. Our biophysical twins help us study how the variations in our biology and the social and environmental conditions of our lives relate to brain function,” explained Ibáñez. “The importance of biophysical brain twins is that they connect what brain scans record with the underlying processes that could produce those signals. Each twin acts as a personalised virtual laboratory: researchers can adjust how its neural populations interact and examine how those changes affect the whole brain. This opens a route from observing differences to testing possible explanations, mechanisms, potential treatments and interventions.”.

In a recent development, “MRI records indirect measures of neural activity. Biophysical twins let us simulate the neural processes that might generate those signals and explore why they differ from person to person,” added Herzog.

Applying these nearly 7,000 personalized models across diverse clinical cohorts exposed clear mechanistic boundaries between normal aging and dementia:.

To overcome the historical divide between neuroimaging and real-world lived context, the team linked individual brain models with macro-level environmental indicators across 10 domains alongside personal socioeconomic histories.

It has been revealed that robust associations emerged in seven of the ten environmental domains, most prominently in indicators measuring democratic conditions (free choices, civic participation, political representation, and rule of law), soil and water quality, and air pollution. Complementary analyses of individual life circumstances further linked brain dynamics to healthcare access, childhood experiences, and financial stability. These relationships persisted even after controlling for age, sex, clinical diagnosis, country, and MRI scanner hardware.

By releasing their open-source code and model parameters, the authors have established a global testbed for in silico experimentation. Future studies can overlay neurotransmitter receptor maps onto these digital twins—simulating how targeted modulation of glutamate (excitatory) or GABA (inhibitory) signaling, or public health improvements in air quality and healthcare access, might shift an aging brain back toward healthy functional patterns.

What is a biophysical “digital brain twin”?

A digital brain twin is a personalized computer simulation built from an individual’s fMRI scan using biological equations. By modeling how 90 connected brain regions interact, it allows researchers to estimate underlying cellular processes, such as the balance between signals that excite or inhibit neurons—and test virtual treatments safely on a computer.

How do brain dynamics differ between normal aging and dementia?

In the study of nearly 7,000 people, normal aging primarily changed how regularly or unpredictably brain activity fluctuated over time. In contrast, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal degeneration disrupted overall activity levels, variability, and the balance between excitatory and inhibitory brain signals all at once.

Can environmental and social conditions really affect how the brain functions?

Sources indicate that yes. Even after accounting for age, sex, diagnosis, and scanner differences, researchers found that environmental factors, especially democratic conditions, soil and water quality, air pollution, healthcare access, and financial circumstances, were measurably linked to underlying simulated brain dynamics.

Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.

Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics.

Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

Recent findings suggest that personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes.

It has been revealed that associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research.

These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • Sources indicate that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Fresh York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

According to recent reports, the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Sources indicate that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

According to recent reports, the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1986 for $1m.

Industry observers note that gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

It has been revealed that A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Latest York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

Industry observers note that french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Major name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

It has been revealed that picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

The Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Recent findings suggest that willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in Fresh York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Recent findings suggest that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Fresh Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article noted the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

Industry observers note that it hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Sources indicate that though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export problems, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

Recent findings suggest that “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

Breaking: The Brain Creates Body Ownership Before Touch Occurs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body.
  • Recent findings suggest that we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us.
  • While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have mapped the exact millisecond-by-millisecond sequence of brain activity that creates the feeling that a hand belongs to our own body. The magnetoencephalography (MEG) study reveals three distinct neural phases, beginning even before physical touch occurs, and explains why right-hemisphere strokes frequently cause patients to disown their left arm.

Recent findings suggest that we effortlessly take for granted that our hands, arms, and limbs belong to us. Yet this seamless sense of body ownership is an active perceptual construction, one that requires the brain to continuously merge visual, tactile, and spatial signals in real time, and one that can shatter dramatically following neurological injury.

While prior neuroimaging studies identified the general brain regions involved in self-perception, the exact temporal choreography, when each region activates and how signals cascade across the cortex, has remained elusive.

Now, in a study published in Nature Communications, neuroscientists at Karolinska Institutet led by Professor Henrik Ehrsson (Department of Neuroscience) and co-author Professor Daniel Lundqvist (Department of Clinical Neuroscience) have charted the birth of body ownership millisecond by millisecond.

To capture how the brain constructs the feeling that a limb is its own, the team recruited 45 healthy volunteers for a precision robotic version of the classic rubber hand illusion.

In a recent development, participants watched a lifelike artificial hand resting in front of them while their real left hand remained hidden behind a screen. Two robotic arms delivered brief, synchronized touches to both the visible rubber hand and the concealed real hand, while high-speed magnetoencephalography (MEG) recorded whole-brain magnetic fields. By comparing synchronized touches (which trigger the illusion that the rubber hand is part of one’s body) against asynchronous touches and real-hand control conditions, the researchers isolated the neural signature of body ownership across the 28 participants who vividly experienced the illusion.

Reconstructing brain activity every four milliseconds produced a real-time movie of self-perception unfolding across three distinct phases:.

Sources indicate that “We know quite a lot about which areas of the brain are involved in the sense that the body is our own, but considerably less about when different areas become active and how they interact. We have now been able to track how activity patterns in the brain develop over time,” explained Ehrsson.

It has been revealed that “The fact that the activity began even before the hand was touched indicates that the brain’s expectations of what we are going to feel are closely linked to the conscious experience of the body as our own,” added Lundqvist. “This study shows when, in what order, and how different brain regions help combine information from different senses into a unified experience of our own body.”.

Notably, during the first two phases of the sequence, neural activity was confined almost entirely to the right hemisphere. This lateralized timing aligns strikingly with clinical neurology: following a stroke, patients who experience somatoparaphrenia, the disturbing condition in which a limb no longer feels like part of one’s own body, almost always disown their left arm after damage to the right hemisphere.

“When stroke patients lose the sense that an arm belongs to them, it is usually the left arm that is affected, following damage to the right hemisphere of the brain,” Ehrsson noted. “In future studies, we want to compare patterns of brain activity associated with the right and left hands to better understand the different roles of the brain’s hemispheres. We also want to collaborate with stroke researchers to investigate this phenomenon in patients.”.

How does the brain create the feeling that your hand belongs to your body?

It has been revealed that karolinska Institutet researchers found that body ownership arises through a precise three-stage sequence of brain activity. It starts with predictive expectation before a hand is even touched, sweeps rapidly across the right frontal, parietal, and cerebellar regions, and finally engages the left hemisphere to unify sensory information.

Why did brain activity start before the hand was physically touched?

Recent findings suggest that seeing an object approach the hand triggers predictive brain activity based on what we expect to feel. This pre-touch expectation primes the brain to merge sight and touch into the conscious experience that the limb is our own.

How does this study help explain disturbed body perception after a stroke?

Because the first two critical stages of body ownership occur almost exclusively in the brain’s right hemisphere, damage to that side from a stroke disrupts the early multisensory integration needed to recognize the left arm, explaining why stroke patients frequently lose the sense that their left arm belongs to them.

Funding: The study was funded by the Swedish Research Council, the Göran Gustafsson Foundation, the Torsten Söderberg Foundation and the Swedish Brain Foundation. NatMEG receives support from the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation. The researchers declare no conflicts of interest.

Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.

We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership?

Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership.

Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm.

Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms.

These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

What a Fictional Robot Can Teach Us About Care

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.
  • In a recent development, the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie.
  • But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This essay contains mild spoilers for the novel Klara and the Sun.

In a recent development, the baby, my baby, was to be named Josie. Josie Joy.

But when she was born, she was decidedly not a Josie. The name was too soft, too ethereal for such a sentient, wide-awake, bird-like baby. I knew that I had to find a newly introduced name. Who are you? I whispered into the swirls of her astoundingly warm, circulated, and singularly perfect ear. I couldn’t wait to get to know her.

Industry observers note that in another story, a girl named Josie is dying. In Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel Klara and the Sun, Josie has an unknown illness and a prognosis that haunts the pages. Her life exists in the shadow of her sister, Sal, who has already died of the same unarticulated illness, likely caused by an elective genetic alteration procedure known as “lifting.”.

Industry observers note that in Josie’s world, being lifted is the upcoming social currency; those who are lifted are expected to have greater access to both intellectual and economic success. The procedure does not, however, come without risk. When we meet Josie’s mother, she is tasked with the impossible: coping with the impending death of her only remaining child. A death likely resulting from a choice she made as a parent. The ultimate consequence.

In a recent development, klara is a robot purchased by Josie’s mom to be her companion, in part (it is implied) to assuage the guilt she feels. I first read Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun shortly after its debut. Despite being disturbed by some aspects of the dystopian world depicted within, my memory of the novel was poignant. I recalled Klara with particular affection.

Now, the distance between Ishiguro’s dystopian world and our current reality is rapidly collapsing. With the much anticipated film adaptation set to be released this Friday, October 23, and the sudden ubiquity of artificial intelligence in our day-to-day lives, Klara and the Sun is now repositioned as a mirror. If we look closely enough, we might discern what remains uniquely human during this moment of profound technological and social change.

It has been revealed that we are introduced to Klara, the story’s narrator, when Josie’s mom takes her to find an artificial friend, or AF for short. In the novel, AFs confer social standing, but also offer practical assistance—tutoring, companionship, monitoring an ailing child—not unlike the benefits purported by artificial intelligence companies today.

Klara has been patiently waiting, alongside several other AFs, to be chosen. Josie’s mother is the final decider. In a foreboding scene, Josie’s mother commands Klara to reenact Josie’s gait—a test, of sorts—before agreeing to purchase her. It’s the precision of Klara’s mimicry that convinces “the Mother” (as she’s called in the novel) that Klara is the right model for Josie.

All of this, we learn through Klara. Ishiguro’s choice to position the reader within Klara’s perspective allows us to bypass the quagmire question of whether or not Klara is conscious and instead project our own consciousness onto her. In doing so, we view the human world through her sometimes malfunctioning robot eyes, as she nonjudgmentally conveys the complexities of the very flawed and sometimes desperate human behaviors she seeks to understand. In one particularly moving scene, Klara witnesses the vulnerability of caring for another human being:.

I saw before me, on the near edge of the bed, a large shifting shape, made additionally complex by the patches of blackness and moonlight moving over its surface. I realized the shape was the Mother and Josie embracing. . . . As well as their limbs, their hair had become mingled, and then their shape began gently to rock, in a way not unlike when their goodbyes became extended.

According to recent reports, “Don’t want to die, Mom. I don’t want that.”.

“It’s okay. Okay.” The Mother’s voice was soft, at just the same level mine had been.

Recent findings suggest that prior to this moment, Klara—steadfast and ever-available—had offered her presence to comfort Josie. Yet, despite their far more complicated and at times strained relationship, it is the Mother that Josie calls for.

It has been revealed that when I first became a parent, I confided to a friend that when my not-Josie was born, I felt like a latest sun had burst into my solar system, and I was now orbiting around her. I couldn’t quite articulate the “before,” in my metaphor. I didn’t feel like I was previously my own sun, nor did I feel like I was a planet untethered to others. But there was something distinctly different when she arrived, a whole new consciousness, a space and force and awareness created within me. Her pull was intoxicating, undeniable, sometimes terrifying, and my awareness and attention seemed to expand overnight to now include not only my own experiences, but also to track, perceive, anticipate, and accommodate her own.

If Klara had turned to psychological theory and research about the complexity of parent-child bonds, she would have found a great deal of it. Consider Winnicott’s “good-enough mother” or research indicating that parents and infants are rarely, if ever, perfectly attuned, and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the navigation of the ruptures and repairs themselves reinforce attachment. It has become increasingly clear through evolving applications of experiments such as Edward Tronick’s now famous “still-face” experiment that the imperfect dance between caregiver and child lays the groundwork for resilience and emotional regulation.

In The Philosophical Baby, developmental psychologist and philosopher Alison Gopnik indicates, “It’s not so much that we care for children because we love them, as that we love them because we care for them.”.

We love them because we care for them.

Beyond Gopnik’s own research, there is an abundance of data to back this up. Studies I have long been familiar with, such as those demonstrating that in same-sex, non-carrying male couples, fathers who act as primary parents show changes in similar brain regions to women who carried their pregnancies and go on to parent their children. Yet, there was something profound about the simplicity of Gopnik’s statement, about love being something we cultivate within ourselves and, more precisely, about care being the means through which we build love, not merely a necessary byproduct.

Recent findings suggest that in a separate interview, Gopnik jokes that spending time with a three-year-old gives you a small taste of sainthood. Not in the sense that the demands are so extreme that you inherently become a saint (though there is a real argument to be made here for any parent who weathers the storm of a parking lot tantrum), but in the actual felt-sense of the divine, the experience of feeling so acutely and utterly in love with this being, so in awe of their singularity, their specialness, their openness to experience, their brilliance.

Sources indicate that gopnik continues on, teasing, about our tendency to claim the uniqueness of our three-year-old, in her case her grandchild, but gently affirms the truth beneath: that there is something numinous, universal, pure within all three-year-olds, a near-magical vitality that we sometimes make contact with when we intimately care for one. Something primal, or perhaps primary, is awoken when we re-experience the world through the eyes of a three-year-old.

My not-Josie is now three. In many ways she is more unknowable, separate, than she was when she was a newborn, so physically attached and dependent on me. Now, she has her own relationships—with teachers, classmates, family members—that are entirely her own. And yet, she occupies and orients so much of me, continually changing my experience of the world, my access to play, to awe, to unadulterated, intoxicating adoration.

This past summer, I was sitting by a lake, relaxed but hawk-eyed as I watched my not-Josie from the shore. I felt a familiar presence by my side, the barely-perceptible shadow in my peripheral vision of a small body sitting down, and soon thereafter, the unselfconscious weight of a small hand on my leg. I looked down to see a head covered in feathery blonde hair, not the dark, curly brown of my own child.

Sources indicate that the wispy tufts belonged to another small child who had clearly mistaken me for her mother. In that brief moment before she looked up, before we both acknowledged our separateness, I felt overcome with the awareness—as though received through the touch of her hand on my leg—that her mother loved her in the way that I love my child, and that, despite how unbelievably special my not-Josie is, my love for her is not. It is precious, but also universal.

It has been revealed that intellectually, of course, this is not a profound realization. Emotionally touching into it is, on the other hand, equally as brutal as it is beautiful. Next to this small child, healthy and safe, I felt her preciousness, but also that of all the children flooding my news feed every day who are not healthy and safe, and whose parents must live with this love and that devastation.

On the back cover, Klara and the Sun is described as a story about love, which it undeniably is. But I think it’s perhaps more fundamentally about care.

Care is arguably more tangible than love, but also more complex, friction-prone, messy. It’s the gaps, the mistakes, the harms, the repairs, the precarity, the forgiving, that make care so deeply painful and so deeply nourishing. Nourishing enough to sustain the vulnerability of love.

It is care that drives Josie’s mother to have her “lifted” in an age-old attempt of desperation to give her child what she perceives as the best chance at a full life in a rapidly reorganizing world. It is care that sends the Mother down the path of trying to find a way to have Klara “continue” Josie’s life, even though she has already tried and failed to recreate her first child’s consciousness in an artificial intelligence through the work of an artist and scientist named Capaldi.

Sources indicate that it is care that allows the Mother—despite her cold exterior—to fearlessly comfort her child as she confronts the possibility of her own death, enveloping her, rocking her, soothing her through the unimaginable. It is the Mother’s human care, not her cowardice, that makes her love true.

There is so much in Klara and the Sun that is undeniably relevant in this particular social, cultural, and technological moment, so many ways in which Ishiguro’s Josie and my not-Josie’s world are suddenly uncomfortably proximate, but it is what Klara herself affirms about humanity that is most resonant.

At the end of the novel, Klara reflects on what she’s learned. She did not have to become a Josie 2.0, for Josie survived. Klara is glad for this, of course, believing that it was her bargain with the Sun (which she sees as a kind of god) that saved Josie. Sitting discarded in a junk yard, Klara is increasingly convinced that the desperate blueprint to turn Josie into a digital consciousness wouldn’t have worked:.

It has been revealed that mr. Capaldi believed there was nothing special inside Josie that couldn’t be continued. He told the Mother he’d searched and searched and found nothing like that. But I believe now he was searching in the wrong place. There was something very special, but it wasn’t inside Josie. It was inside those who loved her. That’s why I think now Mr. Capaldi was wrong and I wouldn’t have succeeded.

It is what happens within us and between us when we care for another being that differentiates us as humans. In other words, it’s not so much what’s there but what’s not there—the space between the person in front of us and how we perceive, imperfectly care for, and ultimately love them—that makes us human.

It has been revealed that through Klara’s eyes, I was able to see more clearly what connects the Mother and her Josie to me and my not-Josie. It is the very fact that we can so wholeheartedly love another being, without being them, having them, solving them, knowing every bit of them. It is the fact that still, we carry them in our hearts, and somehow we are not heavier for it.

Liza Ruggiero, M.A. , ACC, is a leadership coach, facilitator, educator, and writer whose work draws on psychology, mindfulness, and emotional intelligence to support personal and professional growth. She is the founder of Heartwork Leadership Practice, where she helps people navigating transitions, such as emerging leaders, upcoming parents, and career changers, develop the self-awareness and self-regard to lead from a place of purpose.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues.
  • For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s.
  • Industry observers note that against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New neuroscience research reveals that both psilocybin and ketamine improve decision accuracy by helping the brain rely less on rigid, repetitive habits and more on real-time sensory cues. The study shows that rather than scrambling neural signaling, these compounds gently sculpt ongoing brain activity, trading a slight reduction in reaction speed for sharper, more flexible choices.

For the roughly one in five Americans living with a mental health condition, frontline psychiatric medications have changed remarkably little since the 1950s. Conventional antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) often require weeks to take effect, demand chronic daily use, and fail to provide adequate relief for roughly 30% of patients with treatment-resistant depression.

Industry observers note that against this backdrop, psychedelic compounds, including classic serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin and dissociative agents like ketamine, have sparked intense clinical excitement for their ability to produce rapid, durable improvements in mood, addiction, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Yet precisely how these drugs alter neural circuits to break entrenched patterns of negative thinking has remained poorly understood.

Now, in a study published in Science Advances, neuroscientists at Boston University led by assistant professor Dr. Benjamin Scott and associate professor Dr. Steve Ramirez have uncovered a shared pro-cognitive mechanism linking psilocybin and ketamine: both drugs weaken the brain’s reliance on automatic habits and heighten sensitivity to immediate sensory cues.

To test how psychedelics influence moment-to-moment decision-making, Scott, Ramirez, and colleagues trained mice on a perceptual task requiring the animals to use brief pulses of light to identify which of two ports contained a reward.

Industry observers note that untreated mice performed the task moderately well, but frequently fell into habitual traps—repeatedly returning to a previously rewarded location even when the light cues clearly signaled a change. Following administration of either psilocybin or ketamine, however, mice made significantly fewer errors. Rather than falling back on repetitive choice biases, treated animals anchored their decisions much more closely to real-time sensory information.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” explained Scott, a faculty member in Boston University’s Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

Although psilocybin acts primarily on serotonin receptors (such as 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A) while ketamine blocks glutamate NMDA receptors, their behavioral effects converged on sharper, less biased decision-making.

To observe what changed inside the brain, the researchers combined brain-wide genetic activity mapping with targeted neural recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a prefrontal region essential for evaluating rewards, making decisions, and updating beliefs when rules change.

According to recent reports, remarkably, psilocybin did not erase or scramble existing task representations. Instead, core OFC activity patterns tracking sensory cues and choices remained largely intact, accompanied by widespread yet subtle adjustments across interconnected brain regions. According to the authors, this gentle sculpting of ongoing neural activity aligns closely with clinical observations that a person’s mindset and environment (“set and setting”) strongly shape the psychedelic experience.

The team also identified an important behavioral nuance: while mice made more accurate choices after receiving psilocybin or ketamine, they took longer to deliberate, revealing a classic speed-accuracy tradeoff. While slower deliberation can benefit reflective cognitive therapy, it underscores why activities demanding split-second reaction times, such as driving, are unsafe under the influence of these compounds.

Looking ahead, Scott and Ramirez proposal to pinpoint the exact neural pathways responsible for breaking rigid habits, with the ultimate goal of developing targeted, next-generation therapies that unlock cognitive flexibility without hallucinogenic side effects.

How do psilocybin and ketamine improve decision-making in this study?

Boston University researchers found that both drugs help the brain pay closer attention to immediate sensory cues (like flashes of light) while reducing the tendency to fall back on repetitive habits, leading to significantly more accurate choices.

Do psychedelics scramble normal brain activity during a task?

No. Recordings in the orbitofrontal cortex indicated that the brain’s core patterns for tracking cues and making decisions remained largely preserved. Instead of causing chaos, psilocybin induced widespread yet subtle shifts that gently sculpted how the brain updated its beliefs.

Were there any downsides to the improved decision accuracy?

In a recent development, yes. Researchers observed a speed-accuracy tradeoff: while treated animals made fewer mistakes, they took longer to make their decisions, suggesting these compounds slow down reaction times even as they promote more deliberative thinking.

Psychedelics Shift Decision Strategies and Reconfigure Orbitofrontal Dynamics.

Psychedelics such as psilocybin and ketamine are attracting renewed attention as rapid-acting therapeutics, yet how they reshape cognitive computations remains poorly understood.

According to recent reports, to address this, we trained mice on a free-response perceptual decision-making task that disentangles bias-driven from sensory-guided strategies. Acute administration of psilocybin or ketamine slowed decision times while improving accuracy. Behavioral modeling combining drift diffusion and GLM-HMM approaches revealed that these effects were driven by increased decision thresholds and a shift toward sensory-engaged states.

Whole-brain c-Fos mapping identified modulation of distributed task-related networks, including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC). Calcium imaging demonstrated that OFC population dynamics were reorganized under psychedelic conditions, with preserved task selectivity but altered temporal structure and shifted population correlations.

Together, these findings indicate that psychedelics shift decision-making toward greater reliance on sensory evidence while reshaping cortical population dynamics, providing a system-level account of their effects on perceptual decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

These foods contain both fibre and protein, which may help explain why they were linked to weight loss.

Beans, lentils and chickpeas may help people lose weight and trim their waistlines, according to a review of 36 randomised trials.

Adults who ate diets containing these foods lost about a kilogram more than those on comparison diets.

Their waists also shrank by about 1.6 centimetres more on average.

One reason may be that beans and lentils deliver both fibre and protein, which can help a meal feel more filling.

If people feel satisfied after eating, they may find it easier to eat less later in the day.

The researchers brought together trials in which adults were randomly assigned to diets containing legumes other than soya or to a comparison diet.

The trials covered a range of pulses, including dried beans, peas, chickpeas and lentils.

That makes the findings relevant to several familiar foods, although the pooled result tells us little about how a serving of lentils stacks up against a serving of chickpeas.

The researchers looked at body weight, waist circumference, body fat and body mass index, which relates a person’s weight to their height.

The results pointed to modest reductions in weight and waist size, with a reduction in body fat in the trials that measured it.

A bowl of lentil soup and a bowl of soup made with refined grains can feel quite different to eat, partly because lentils bring fibre and protein to the meal.

The researchers suggest that these nutrients could help people feel satisfied and reduce how much they go on to eat.

What the beans or lentils replace may matter as well.

Replacing some of the rice in a meal with chickpeas gives you a different mix of foods from adding chickpeas to your usual portion of rice.

That distinction helps explain why the comparison diets matter when interpreting the results.

The study was published in the journal Food Science & Nutrition (Rahmanian et al., 2026).

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes. Tracking nearly 3,000 adults from age 18 into their mid-50s, researchers found lower memory, processing speed, and executive function scores among those with rising glucose trajectories, alongside structural brain changes in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes.

Source: American Heart Association.

While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.

Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.

Sources indicate that led by first author Dr. Regina Paradela (postdoctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School and neuroepidemiologist at the Global Brain Health Institute at UC San Francisco) and senior author Dr. Kristine Yaffe (director of the Center for Population Brain Health at UC San Francisco), the study tracked metabolic and cognitive trajectories across 2,808 participants in the landmark Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort.

It has been revealed that enrolled between 1985 and 1986 at ages 18 to 30 across four U.S. cities, participants underwent repeated fasting blood glucose measurements over 30 years until reaching an average age of 55. At the 30-year mark, all participants completed comprehensive neuropsychological testing, and a subset of 605 participants underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

By mapping longitudinal glucose patterns across the 2,463 participants who remained free of Type 2 diabetes, the researchers identified three distinct metabolic trajectories:.

An additional 345 participants developed Type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL) during the 30-year follow-up.

Even after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, both the increasing-glucose group and the Type 2 diabetes group performed significantly worse on tests of memory, processing speed, executive function, and global cognition compared with the lower-stable glucose group.

“The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very notable,” explained Paradela. “This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about.”.

Furthermore, MRI scans revealed tangible anatomical footprints among participants who developed Type 2 diabetes, who exhibited less total gray matter and more abnormal white matter tissue, markers closely tied to accelerated brain aging and cognitive decline.

“Future research should evaluate whether monitoring and managing increasing glucose levels earlier in adulthood can prevent or delay cognitive decline and structural brain changes,” said senior author Yaffe.

It has been revealed that commenting on the study, Dr. Elisabeth Marsh, professor of neurology at The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chair of the writing group for the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement Brain Health Across the Life Span, emphasized the value of early vascular and metabolic care: “The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 offers steps to improve heart and brain health and support cognitive well-being at every stage of life.”.

Can rising blood sugar harm brain health even if you don’t have diabetes?

Industry observers note that yes. Over a 30-year study, young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually increased into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse on midlife tests of memory, processing speed, and executive function than peers whose blood sugar remained low and stable, even though they never developed Type 2 diabetes.

What structural brain changes were seen in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes?

MRI brain scans revealed that adults who developed Type 2 diabetes by their mid-50s had less total gray matter volume and more abnormal white matter tissue compared to those who maintained lower-stable blood sugar levels from young adulthood.

When should adults start paying attention to blood sugar for brain protection?

Recent findings suggest that researchers note that changes in glucose metabolism begin affecting cognitive performance much earlier than age 65. Monitoring and managing blood sugar trajectories starting in young adulthood, using healthy nutrition, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk control, may help protect midlife and late-life brain health.

Funding: Co-authors, disclosures and funding sources are listed in the manuscript.

Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age.

Research on associations between long‐term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.

Participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

Sources indicate that we included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower‐stable (n=1387), moderate‐stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower‐stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.

Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every year, we invite staff and regular contributors to nominate TV series for Greater Goodies, the awards we give to stories that exemplify or illustrate kindness, community, empathy, and more keys to well-being. Here’s what we came up with this year: The Boroughs, Death by Lightning, Envidiosa, The Hawk, Heated Rivalry, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Lucky, Murderbot, Pluribus, and Shrinking.

Industry observers note that name the last show you’ve seen that features a hero over the age of 60. Drawing a blank? It’s not your fault—the media’s modus operandi is to equate heroism with youthfulness. Netflix’s The Boroughs flips this stereotype on its head.

With a star-studded lead cast, all 70 or older, we follow Sam Cooper’s (Alfred Molina) experience as he reluctantly moves into a senior living community in Newly introduced Mexico after the death of his wife. But a series of strange events suggests that this is no ordinary retirement community.

It has been revealed that as Sam navigates grief, new friendships, and a new identity, he joins forces with his neighbors to solve and resolve the community mystery. Overcoming obstacles like age discrimination and self-doubts, the group peels back the layers of the strange occurrences. At the root of the mystery is a societal fear of aging.

Sources indicate that the show highlights what researcher Margie Lachman calls “crystallized intelligence”: the culmination of life experience, memory, and know-how. In The Boroughs, that turns out to be just as heroic as super human strength or the ability to fly. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

In a recent development, history has already told us how Death by Lightning ends: Charles Guiteau will assassinate President James Garfield in 1881. But why? That’s one of the questions explored by the series, and it finds motivation in a sense of purpose–how purpose forms and how people come to cross-purposes.

Garfield (Michael Shannon) is principled and drawn reluctantly into a presidential contest he entered to nominate someone else. Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), meanwhile, is disturbingly sympathetic: charming, articulate, and desperate to do something meaningful with his life. Despite failed ventures, including a stint at the Oneida free-love commune, he remains convinced greatness awaits him. Believing his campaigning secured Garfield’s victory, he expects a government position to confirm his worth.

Sources indicate that as their stories converge, Garfield finds purpose in his presidency: fighting corruption while supporting education and equal opportunity. Guiteau pursues a reward he feels he deserves, an entitlement that leads to tragedy.

In these ways, Garfield and Guiteau offer sharply contrasting answers to what makes a life meaningful, and watching their stories unfold side by side, we see how differently the desire to matter can play out.

Industry observers note that who you really ought to be watching closely is Garfield’s Vice President, Chester A. Arthur (Nick Offerman). A comfortable beneficiary of the political machine, he becomes an unlikely source of hope as the story goes on. Offerman makes him funny, flawed, and increasingly affecting as the demands of office begin to collide with old loyalties.

Recent findings suggest that in a political landscape that can leave us cynical–in both the 19th century and the 21st–the series makes room for something more hopeful: the possibility that even an unlikely person can rise to the occasion, if they know why they need to rise. – Aurelia Santos.

When almost-40-year-old Vicky (Griselda Siciliani) breaks up with her long-term boyfriend, she is driven to embark upon a journey of self-discovery.

At first, Vicky is just looking for a replacement for her boyfriend—but the problem is that her compulsive comparisons with other women sabotage attempts to connect with other people. (Indeed, the name of this Argentinian show, Envidiosa, means “envious.”) Vicky is self-absorbed and yet at the same time she doesn’t have a strong sense of her own self.

We see this vividly in her hilarious sessions with her therapist. When, for example, she goes on an envious rant about a friend’s milestone, she is forced to confront the quiet, uncomfortable realization that she never once asked how her friend actually felt. In short, Vicky is not a polished role model—and over the course of four seasons, we see her empathy grow through the painful process of unlearning self-centeredness.

According to recent reports, personally, I see Envidiosa as an opportunity to question how we show up for others’ joys and struggles, and I take it as an invitation to reflect: How can I empathize with the ups and downs of those around me? Envidiosa is a funny and at times embarrassingly relatable story about trying to become a more empathic human being and friend. — Criss Cuervo.

In The Hawk, washed-up professional golfer Lonnie “The Hawk” Hawkins (Will Ferrell) has made a miracle comeback into the PGA tour—this time around, facing a tough competitor in his son, Lance (Jimmy Tatro).

Recent findings suggest that it’s a screwball comedy, full of dirty jokes and a rapid-fire rapport between Lonnie and his not-quite-ex-wife, Stacy (Molly Shannon). A makeshift-caddy he “picked up at Walmart” (while chatting up the parking lot, from his camper van) adds to the fun, serving up an unlikely duo that seem happy just to be alive.

Recent findings suggest that even when he’s pretty down and out, Lonnie is looking on the bright side of things. Everything is done with gusto—he chats up the golf ball before each swing, he devours plates of Buffalo Wild Wings, he plays mini golf with his son and makes it a full-on competition.

Sources indicate that “Son, never play golf angry,” he tells Lance. For Lonnie, life is all about golf—and golf is all about fun. Why spend all your time on something if you aren’t doing it for the joy of it?

I especially love Lonnie’s adoration for his estranged wife, a firecracker in her own right. In episode four, when the Hawk crashes his son’s engagement party–yes, you read that right–and then attempts a getaway with his caddie in the van, Stacy hurls the cake at them, along with a string of expletives.

According to recent reports, it doesn’t even faze him. “You gotta love the passion!” Lonnie gushes. “That is one hot tamale!” — Hope Reese.

Heated Rivalry follows stick-crossed lovers Shane and Ilya as they figure out how to be intimate within the highly competitive, homophobic environment of professional hockey.

At first, Shane and Ilya swap fluids more readily than emotions. But over the course of six episodes, the two learn to love across gaps in culture, language, and experience. In one pivotal scene, Shane invites Ilya to speak vulnerably about family dynamics in Ilya’s native Russian—despite not understanding a word of it.

Recent findings suggest that that works because Shane does not focus attention on himself. Instead, he stays present on the phone, serving as a witness to Ilya’s visceral emotions. Their connection lies in felt care, in hearing the texture of another’s heartbreak.

It has been revealed that in similar fashion, Ilya grounds Shane in stressful encounters. He supports Shane through panic without wallowing in his lover’s fear and entices Shane to relish pleasures outside of straight standards. As a couple, they help each other explore complex parts of themselves. We see a similar process unfold in another couple in the show, as they learn to respect each other’s different needs.

It has been revealed that people might tune into Heated Rivalry for locker room towel drops and HBO’s glossy cinematography. They should stay to see a couple learn to love each other’s differences. The show exemplifies how bridging differences, at its best, means supporting others to more fully encounter themselves, and how in the process our relationships can grow.

Recent findings suggest that with plenty of additional homoerotic stick-and-ball games to pull on from the novels of Rachel Reid, the next season of Heated Rivalry is expected to air on HBO Max and Canada’s Crave in Spring 2027. — Luke Brown.

Recent findings suggest that the monstrously successful HBO series Game of Thrones famously tossed out a lot of good-and-evil fantasy tropes to tell a morally complicated story of how power corrupts even the best people. A prequel called House of the Dragon shares that worldview.

It has been revealed that that’s why a fresh prequel called A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms came as something of a surprise to fans. Unlike the other two series, this is not a story about a struggle for power. Instead, it focuses on a rather naive, not-too-bright “hedge knight” named Duncan (Peter Claffey) seeking to be hired by whatever lord will take him. Though Duncan is taller and stronger than most, he’s touchingly childlike as he tries to find his place in the merry old kingdoms of Westeros.

The first two episodes are funny and charming, as Duncan acquires a squire in the form of a little bald boy going by the name Egg (Dexter Sol Ansell), and fumblingly tries to enter a jousting tournament. And then Duncan finds himself on a collision course with the great and powerful of Westeros. When violence finally comes, there’s nothing casual about it. We feel the force of every blow, the tragedy of every death, and the erosion of Duncan’s innocence.

Industry observers note that I’m giving A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms the award for integrity, but I can’t tell you why without spoiling the ending. Let’s just say that the series turns out to be the story of how one simple young man discovers what is most important to him—and finds the courage to stick to that path even in the face of isolation, temptations, and threats. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

How do you exit a life you were born into?

That’s the question behind Lucky, starring Anya Taylor-Joy. Lucky was raised by her con-artist father and taught the “family business” from a young age—but when we meet her, she navigating internal conflict with the life she’s been told to live and the life she wants for herself.

Sources indicate that her desire to quit is complicated by her marriage to Cary, the son of a ruthless mob leader, who was also socialized into a life of crime. The couple initiative one final con as their exit strategy, but it goes terribly wrong. Lucky sets out to resolve the botched plan, reconcile her marriage, and protect both her life and her father’s.

Sources indicate that her intelligence is put to the test as she puts the pieces together, connects the dots, and outsmarts her rivals. In the process she discovers her own virtue—and that the intelligence which made her a successful con artist can also set her free.

According to recent reports, through the course of the series, she realizes that she does not have to pay for the sins of her father. Having never been given the opportunity for self-determination, she makes peace in the best way she knows how and chooses a new path. — Shanna B. Tiayon.

The Murderbot Diaries are a series of science-fiction novellas by Martha Wells, about a genderless, robotic soldier who manages to achieve free will. Since discovery will result in deactivation and since it doesn’t like humans very much anyway, Murderbot conceals its freedom of mind and consumes a lot of human-made entertainment inside its own head, even as it externally follows every order given to it by the evil corporation that owns it. Murderbot even has a favorite TV show: the Star-Trek-like Rise and Fall of Sanctuary Moon.

As a result of this isolation, the novellas are built almost entirely around its memorable inner monologues, with a voice that is by turns snarky, vulnerable, cold-blooded, disgusted, and puzzled. One of the things that makes these books distinctive is that Murderbot is not Pinocchio—it has no wish to become a “real boy.” It doesn’t want a gender, or the same feelings and drives as people. It just wants to be itself—and to have that difference respected.

According to recent reports, while the Apple TV show based on the books is not quite that original or interesting, Murderbot retains its focus on finding the balance between belonging and difference. When we meet Murderbot (Alexander Skarsgård), he’s been hired to protect a group of polyamorous hippie scientists who hail from a utopian colony that exists independently of the corporations that rule the rest of the galaxy.

They are Murderbot’s first encounter with humans not shaped by dehumanizing hyper-capitalistic values, and they observe Murderbot in a way the corporate humans cannot. Over the course of the first season, they begin to realize that there is more to Murderbot than meets the eye, and they learn to see and appreciate Murderbot on its own terms. But what’s crucial is not that they perceive the humanity in the not-human Murderbot—it’s that Murderbot sees the humanity (and the goodness) in them.

It has been revealed that in time, it becomes an accepted part of their society, without becoming more like them. Even so, the first season concludes on a tough-minded, melancholy note, as Murderbot itself can’t quite feel like it belongs. Will it someday find a place among these crunchy idealists? Stay tuned: The second season is coming in 2027. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

Have you ever been among people but you didn’t feel part of the crowd? Like they were in on a joke that you just couldn’t get?

It has been revealed that welcome to Carol Sturka’s world. The science-fiction premise of Pluribus is that an alien virus transforms humanity into one substantial happy hive mind—everyone except Carol and 13 other people who seem to have immunity.

Even among those remaining individuals, though, Carol stands out as a malcontent. We sense that she’s been a fish out of water for her whole life.

Indeed, not every viewer will find Carol relatable or likable. When we first meet her, she’s at a bookstore event promoting her highly successful romantasy series. With her fans, she’s charming, funny, and kind. When she gets into a limo after a massive sendoff by readers, the driver asks if she’s famous.

Industry observers note that “That depends,” Carol replies. “Are you a massive fan of mindless crap?”.

In short, Carol hates herself, her work, and her readers. And as we discover, her personality is snarky, uptight, stubborn, and uncompromising. When the virus hits, it’s an apocalyptic event, but Carol doesn’t change one bit—and her traits become both a blessing and a curse. The whole world wants to be kind to her, but Carol can’t accept kindness. That drives her to fight back. And that’s what ultimately makes her the hero of the story.

In the end, Pluribus is a very Greater Good thought experiment. It takes prosociality to its limits and finds that a total togetherness, empathy, and cooperation to the exclusion of selfishness, crankiness, and boundaries is a self-destructive dystopia, not a utopia. The show seems to argue that humanity needs difficult people like Carol to survive, and so invites us to appreciate what the Carols of the world have to offer. — Jeremy Adam Smith.

In Shrinking, talking and listening are the name of the game. Jimmy (Jason Segel) is a widowed psychotherapist who helps patients navigate anxiety, OCD, PTSD, and other ailments as he himself is floundering.

According to recent reports, but he’s not alone. His teenage daughter, overbearing-but-lovable neighbors, and coworker-friends (with Harrison Ford as the curmudgeonly head of the practice) are all there to help him when his life goes off the rails after his wife was killed by a drunk driver.

In its three-season run, the series is heavy-handed with its use of therapy-speak among the whole gang, whether between therapist-to-patient, therapist-to-daughter, or therapist-to-therapist. Characters “feel seen.” More times than I can count, they tell each other “I hear you.” We witness, in detail, exchanges inside the therapy office—and outside of it, in a rogue practice known as “Jimmying,” where therapy takes place at such venues as, for instance, the boxing ring.

Industry observers note that in other words, there’s a lot of “deep listening”: the practice of being present, open, and empathic with another person, in a way that goes beyond just hearing and understanding words. In his grief, Jimmy himself is not always a perfect deep listener. He tends to talk more than a typical therapist, and frequently injects himself into the discussion. Shrinking isn’t about perfection—it’s about struggling to connect and growing in the process. – Hope Reese.

Why Nerve Pain Lingers

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury.
  • Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
  • For millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury. The multi-omics and electrophysiological study reveals that nerve injury suppresses the nuclear regulatory protein Nono, triggering a steep drop in Kcnq2 potassium channels that normally calm spinal pain neurons, while restoring Nono reverses pain hypersensitivity in animal models.

Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

For millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed. Rather than stemming solely from ongoing tissue damage at the original wound site, persistent nerve pain is frequently driven by central sensitization, a state in which pain-processing circuits inside the spinal cord become hyperexcitable and amplify ordinary sensory signals.

Now, a comprehensive study published in Research by scientists at Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Fudan University, and partner institutions has pinpointed a critical molecular switch behind this spinal hyperexcitability: the Nono–Kcnq2 regulatory axis.

By combining five layers of molecular profiling with single-neuron electrophysiology and behavioral testing, the team demonstrated how nerve injury silences a vital genetic brake inside spinal neurons—and showed that restoring this pathway alleviates chronic pain sensitivity.

Under healthy conditions, neurons in the spinal cord’s dorsal horn rely on specialized potassium channels to stabilize their electrical charge and prevent runaway firing. When potassium ions flow out of a neuron, they keep excitability in check; when those channels disappear, neurons fire rapidly in response to minimal stimulation.

According to recent reports, to trace why potassium channel control breaks down after nerve trauma, the investigators examined a rat model of chronic sciatic nerve constriction, which produces pronounced mechanical and thermal pain sensitivity within three days. Electrophysiological recordings confirmed that spinal dorsal horn neurons fired far more readily while exhibiting sharply diminished outward potassium currents.

Applying an integrated multi-omics pipeline, spanning proteomics, phosphoproteomics, transcription factor profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing across 48,279 spinal cord cells, the researchers mapped the exact cellular shifts occurring at seven and 21 days post-injury:.

Molecular binding experiments confirmed that Nono directly binds to a conserved region of the Kcnq2 gene promoter to drive its expression. To test whether repairing this broken link could relieve pain, the researchers delivered an adenoviral vector carrying Nono into the spinal region of nerve-injured rats.

Increasing Nono expression successfully rebuilt Kcnq2 protein abundance, restored protective outward potassium currents in dorsal horn neurons, and significantly eased mechanical and thermal pain hypersensitivity. When the team applied XE991, a selective pharmacological blocker of Kcnq2/3 potassium channels, both the restored potassium currents and the behavioral pain relief were largely reversed, confirming that Nono alleviates pain specifically by reactivating Kcnq2 channels.

While the researchers emphasize that clinical therapies remain a long-term goal—noting that experiments were conducted in male rats and that additional pathways also contribute to neuropathic pain—the findings illuminate a clear mechanistic bridge linking gene transcription to electrical excitability in the spinal cord.

Rather than merely masking pain signals with broad analgesics, future therapies aimed at preserving Nono activity or supporting Kcnq2 potassium channel function could help quiet overactive spinal circuits at their molecular source.

Why can neuropathic pain persist even after a nerve injury has healed?

Following nerve trauma, neurons in the spinal cord can undergo central sensitization, becoming abnormally excitable so that they amplify harmless signals like light touch or mild warmth into intense pain.

What did researchers discover about the Nono and Kcnq2 proteins in the spinal cord?

According to recent reports, scientists found that nerve injury reduces the activity of the nuclear protein Nono, which normally switches on the Kcnq2 gene. Kcnq2 produces potassium channels that act like electrical brakes to calm spinal neurons; when Kcnq2 levels drop by up to 80%, pain neurons fire excessively.

Did restoring Nono reduce pain sensitivity in the animal study?

Yes. When researchers used a viral vector to restore Nono expression in the spinal cord of rats with nerve injuries, Kcnq2 potassium channel levels rebounded, neuronal firing calmed down, and the animals highlighted significantly less sensitivity to mechanical and thermal pain.

Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Nono–Kcnq2 Regulation of Neuronal Excitability in Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain.

Neuropathic pain, resulting from somatosensory nervous system damage or disease, is a debilitating condition marked by spontaneous pain, hypersensitivity, and sensory abnormalities. Neuropathic pain involves spinal neuronal hyperexcitability, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined.

We utilized a comprehensive multi-omics approach, incorporating proteomics, phosphoproteomics, concatenated tandem array of consensus transcription response elements, and both single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, to chart time-resolved adaptations in the L4 to L6 spinal cord of a chronic constriction injury rat model.

Sources indicate that multi-omics revealed remodeling of glutamatergic synapse pathways and identified non-POU (Pit-Oct-Unc) domain-containing octamer binding (Nono) as a down-regulated transcription factor associated with reduced potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (Kcnq2) expression. Nono and Kcnq2 were co-enriched in neurexin 3-positive and peripherin-positive spinal neurons.

It has been revealed that restoring Nono expression up-regulated Kcnq2, enhanced K+ outward currents (an effect largely abolished by the Kcnq2/3 blocker XE991), and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, Nono was enriched at a conserved Kcnq2 promoter region in vivo and enhanced Kcnq2 promoter activity in reporter assays.

Together, these findings established a Nono–Kcnq2 transcriptional axis that constrained spinal excitability and suggested a therapeutic entry point for neuropathic pain.
